own_solution.law: Radiation pressure on a partly reflecting mirror, normal component: F = (I A cos^2(theta)/c)(1 + R); v = F t / m
assumptions: I measured perpendicular to the beam, so intercepted power is I A cos(theta)
absorbed light transfers its normal momentum, specularly reflected light twice it
v << c so Doppler and recoil-angle corrections are negligible
constant force over 24 h, mirror starts at rest

defect_reasons.missing_assumption: TE4B6 and TFEB0 add light from a second lamp without saying it travels along the beam at 30 degrees (or how its 470 W/m^2 is measured); the answer 153.59 m/s assumes it simply raises the beam intensity to 1870 W/m^2, while light from another direction would give a different normal force.

counterexamples: If the second lamp's 470 W/m^2 arrived at normal incidence, its added normal force would be 470*100*1.9/c instead of 470*100*0.75*1.9/c, giving v = 114.99 + 51.10 = 166.09 m/s instead of 153.59 m/s.
notes: F = 1400*100*0.75*1.9/2.998e8 = 6.6544e-4 N; a = 1.33089e-3 m/s^2; v = a*86400 s = 114.99 m/s. With I = 1870 W/m^2 along the beam: v = 114.99*1870/1400 = 153.59 m/s. Photon energy cancels (photon momentum E/c times photon rate P/E). I grade the lamp-direction gap medium because 'adds to the intensity of the light that reaches the mirror' most naturally means the beam intensity rises; if a strict reading of rule 1 is applied it would be high. Earlier-exposure and projection-screen sentences are disconnected.
